description:
We are a team of Systems Engineering students passionate about technology, software development, and solving real-world problems through innovation.

Our interests include web development, Python programming, data analysis, artificial intelligence, machine learning, and working with real-world datasets. We enjoy exploring new technologies, collaborating on challenging projects, and turning ideas into functional solutions.
summary: Pacha Pulse is a field-planning workspace for growers and agricultural advisors. Users can map a field, add the context they know, explore historical temperature and precipitation from NASA POWER, and compare three editable crop-rotation sequences under user-selected rainfall scenarios. A friendly, optional AI companion helps explain the workflow and prepare charts from available evidence; calculations remain on the server, and proposed profile changes require user confirmation. The project makes climate context and rotation trade-offs easier to discuss without presenting a forecast or an automatic planting recommendation. It is important because agricultural decisions depend on local conditions, yet global gridded data cannot replace field measurements or professional judgment. Pacha Pulse therefore shows sources and limitations alongside results: its climate values represent a historical grid point, rainfall scenarios are hypothetical, and the rotation comparison does not predict yield, profitability, soil health, or crop suitability.
details:
What does Pacha Pulse do?

Pacha Pulse is a guided field-planning workspace for growers and agricultural advisors. It brings field context, historical weather, satellite vegetation observations, and crop-rotation ideas into one place. Users can choose a location, draw or import a field outline, record what they know about the farm, and explore evidence one step at a time.

The project connects two NASA data products:

  • NASA POWER daily temperature and precipitation observations for a selected point and historical period.
  • NASA MODIS MOD13Q1 vegetation-index composites (NDVI), with quality flags and missing observations preserved.

A repeatable Mantaro Valley example contains 31 daily NASA POWER observations for January 2025; its derived summary is 60.64 mm of rainfall and a 9.41 °C mean temperature. The separate 2023–2025 MODIS archive contains 69 composites, including 59 usable readings and 10 missing or unreliable readings.

Users can also compare three editable planting sequences, explore a clearly labelled hypothetical rainfall scenario, view charts, and export findings. Optional soil and terrain context is presented separately with its source and limitations. Pacha, the friendly animated guide, explains the workflow. An optional Gemini-powered assistant can explain available evidence and prepare supported charts; ordinary field, weather, and planning tools do not require Gemini.

Pacha Pulse is decision support, not an automated agronomist. Historical grid observations are not measurements from an individual farm or a weather forecast. Satellite composites can include surrounding land, and the experimental NDVI outlook is point-specific, may be unavailable, and has not been validated as a regional farm forecast; the pilot test did not demonstrate strong absolute model fit. Rotation comparisons do not predict yield, profitability, crop suitability, soil health, or irrigation demand.

How does it work?

  1. Set the field context. The user selects a query point or draws/imports a WGS84 field outline, then adds only the farm details they know. A map search moves the map; it does not silently select a field.
  2. Read the evidence. The user explicitly requests historical NASA POWER weather or MODIS vegetation history. The interface keeps the period, source, quality, resolution, and limitations alongside the results. Optional SoilGrids and sampled terrain estimates have their own provenance and do not overwrite the user's field inputs.
  3. Explore alternatives. The user edits a usual planting sequence and two alternatives, then reviews structural differences and, if desired, a rainfall multiplier based on a complete historical total. This is a hypothetical scenario, not a forecast or crop-water estimate.
  4. Review and keep the findings. Users can create charts from available data, export reports, and use Pacha's guided explanations. AI-suggested profile changes require the user to review and confirm them.

What benefits does it have?

  • Makes climate context easier to understand: growers can explore historical rainfall and temperature without having to interpret raw data tables first.
  • Brings multiple kinds of evidence together: NASA weather and satellite vegetation history sit alongside user-provided field context, while optional soil and terrain estimates remain clearly identified as estimates.
  • Encourages comparison rather than unsupported certainty: three editable sequences and explicit assumptions make trade-offs easier to discuss with an advisor.
  • Keeps evidence inspectable: source, dates, quality, missing data, and limitations remain visible; charts can be exported.
  • Supports different users: a simpler guided experience is available for growers, while agronomists can open more technical tables and methods. Both use the same underlying evidence and calculations.
  • Works without the AI companion: core mapping, observations, planning, and manual chart features remain available independently of Gemini.

What is the intended impact?

Pacha Pulse aims to help growers and agricultural advisors have better-informed conversations about a field before making planting or resource decisions. By making historical climate and vegetation context easier to inspect, it can help people identify questions to verify with local knowledge, field measurements, or an agricultural professional.

The intended contribution aligns with:

  • UN Sustainable Development Goal 2 — Zero Hunger: supporting informed, locally reviewed agricultural planning.
  • SDG 12 — Responsible Consumption and Production: making assumptions and evidence visible when comparing possible planting sequences.
  • SDG 13 — Climate Action: helping users explore historical climate context and satellite vegetation observations.

These are intended contributions, not measured project outcomes. Pacha Pulse does not claim that it has increased yields, reduced losses, or changed farmer behavior.

What tools and technologies were used?

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, and Vite.
  • Maps and field geometry: Leaflet / React Leaflet and Turf for user-drawn or imported field outlines and approximate area calculations.
  • Charts and 3D illustrations: Recharts and Three.js.
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, and HTTPX; SQLite is used for local caching and offline data/model workflows.
  • NASA data: NASA POWER daily climate observations and NASA MODIS MOD13Q1 NDVI composites distributed through the ORNL DAAC subset service.
  • Additional context: ISRIC SoilGrids model estimates, Photon place search using OpenStreetMap data, and an elevation service for sampled terrain context.
  • Optional AI: Gemini through a server-side integration with bounded, allowlisted tools. Chart values are calculated by project code, not generated by the model.
  • Offline experimentation: scikit-learn models are trained and evaluated by a separate local worker; HTTP requests do not train a model.
  • Delivery and quality checks: Git/GitHub, automated Python tests, TypeScript/Vite builds, and Playwright browser tests.

How is the project creative?

Pacha Pulse combines scientific evidence with a calm, step-by-step field notebook instead of presenting growers with a dense technical dashboard. A living 3D companion helps orient users, a flat illustrative field makes crop stages tangible, and short lessons translate charts into plain language. Technical users can still inspect the exact values, methods, and source metadata.

The project also makes uncertainty part of the experience: missing observations stay missing, satellite quality flags are retained, and hypothetical scenarios are not presented as predictions. The combination of NASA climate and vegetation data, editable rotation planning, exportable evidence, and a friendly guide is intended to make a technical workflow easier to discuss without hiding its limits.

What factors did the team consider?

  • Scientific reliability: distinguish observations, model estimates, user inputs, scenarios, and experimental predictions; retain quality flags and missing values.
  • Scale and uncertainty: global gridded products and satellite pixels do not describe every small parcel or local microclimate.
  • Usability and accessibility: use a guided sequence, plain-language explanations, responsive layouts, keyboard-accessible controls, and a more detailed agronomist view.
  • Human oversight: preserve user control over field information and require confirmation before applying proposed profile changes.
  • Privacy and operational boundaries: keep the optional Gemini credential on the server; do not imply that a public demo has user accounts or cross-device farm storage.
  • Responsible agricultural advice: do not make unsupported promises about yield, profit, crop suitability, irrigation, soil health, or pest diagnosis.

Who may benefit?

Small and family growers, agricultural advisors and agronomists, agricultural cooperatives, and organizations that support climate-aware farming—especially users who need to combine local knowledge with accessible historical context.
